messages.author: c8e6cf811df8eba2
messages.subject: PLS and CVA
parts:
Hello,

I am currently investigating the possible relationships of 2 independent variables on human facial shape using individual and multiple regression via proc.D.lm function. However since it is my first time using geomorph and kind of new to GMM, I am not sure which way would be the best to investigate this effect. I want to see not only the effect size but the direction of the effect on facial shape.

I wonder if PLS is suitable for exploring this kind of interaction or is there any other kind of analysis that you may recommend. In other softwares (TPS, MorphoJ etc.) it is easy to plot TPS morphs and is possible to see the effect direction using biplot. If PLS is suitable for exploring this kind of interaction, is it possible to observe direction of effect in geomorph?

It is the output of the function summary(PLS). As you can see it provides less information compared to softwares I mentioned (or I do not know how to see them).

  • two.b.pls(A1 = male$coords.coords, A2 = malevariables)



  • r-PLS: 0.472

  • Effect Size (Z): 2.1163

  • P-value: 0.011

  • Based on 1000 random permutations
Another question is that is CVA analysis is suitable for the confirm this kind of hypothesis: "males and females differ significantly in terms of facial shape"? And is mahalanobis distance valid for the describing the effect size?

Thanks,
Fatih

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] PLS and CVA
parts:
Fatih,

 

Whether one uses PLS or regression depends on the nature of the variables you are associating with shape, as well as the hypothesis. PLS describes covariation between sets of variables, while linear models allow for predictions of how shape changes with one or more dependent variables.

 

For all of these, one can generate TPS deformation grids using the ‘shape.predictor’ function in geomorph. The help file provides examples for shape predictions from PCA, regression, anova, PLS and I think a few others.

 

To your last question, differences between males and females is an anova question; also attained via linear models.

 

Best,

 

Dean

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] PLS and CVA
parts:
Fatih,

 

There are two ways to do this. One is visual, and one is more statistical.

 

First, since each relationship is a regression of shape ~ other, one could generate predicted shapes along each regression (e.g., using shape.predictor) and compare these visually for both regressions to see whether shape changes are similar.


Second, this could be accompanied by calculating the angle between vectors of regression coefficients. If this angle is small, it implies the regressions are oriented in similar directions, and hence shape changes implied by these are similar. A permutation test could be used to evaluate this angle.

Dean

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] PLS and CVA
parts:
Fatih,

 

In the geomorph realm, we evaluate angles between vectors using RRPP.  This is a residual permutation procedure, which we used for comparing the angles of vectors for trajectory analysis (e.g., Collyer and Adams 2007); however it has far more uses.

 

If one has performed PLS in geomorph, then one has the permutation scheme as part of the output object. Using the defaults with 999 iterations of the permutation, there is an object with 1000 elements: the first is the observed. One can take the observed PLS vector and obtain the angle between it and your CVA angle.  Then, set up a loop (or a lapply line) which goes through all 1000 components: the observed vs. CVA and the 999 permuted vs. CVA.  That provides you a distribution from which an effect size (Z-score) and a p-value may be obtained.

Dean
